Hacker News #3

The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening

The gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is widening

AI 作者 albertzeyer 热度 694 回复 1015 2026/10/12 04:20
打开原帖 打开外部链接 JSON

摘要

  • Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.
  • - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

I feel like if the gap were so monumental that he could just point to a monument of it, rather than hand-waving at "the vertical professionals".

omnicognate 2026/10/12 19:22
> demolished software and mathematics because those have well-developed verification that's easier than doing the thing itself

They are proving useful for the parts of those things that have that verification, but in neither case is that the whole of the field. In maths, for example, we have seen LLMs find answers to some interesting problems/conjectures, but haven't yet seen them pose any similarly interesting problems/conjectures themselves because the criteria for a "good conjecture" are unclear whereas the criteria for a resolution of an existing conjecture are usually supplied by the conjecture itself.

ndriscoll 2026/10/12 23:30
Did anyone ask? i.e. did anyone with enough background to be able to judge whether a conjecture is "good" just point it at the repo of solved problems and ask it to formulate new conjectures based on the results/proofs? Or ask it to propose new structures to study? Or to identify a previously unknown general technique/tool that it had used in a proof?

It was asked to do a specific thing, and then its brain turned off/was reallocated to something else entirely (e.g. CRUD programming or answering celebrity trivia). It doesn't just idly think in its downtime. If we want it to do something else, we need to ask.

TeMPOraL 2026/10/12 20:09
It did a lot for consumers who dare to use it. It didn't do much for consumers who wait for middleman businesses to offer AI-based services, but that is not because of AI, but existing business model of SaaS.

The businesses pay for tokens and try to deliver their usual enshittified experience, and nothing interesting gets created, because it cannot - enshittification extinguishes all power of AI. Using AI to full extent, in contrast, obviates most need for the business in the first place. So they're all struggling to design an AI powered product, in a world where those very products are already becoming subsumed by AI.

So normies wait for middleware companies to get their shit together or (much more likely) finally die, while people with software experience and eagerness to use AI just don't subscribe, because their favorite LLM handles that work just fine.
